# The Thirty-Seven Letters of Monk Hideo, As Compiled by His Opponent

---

## Editor's Preface

I have arranged these letters in chronological order, as best the postmarks and my own memory allow. Where pages were damaged, I have noted it. Where context seemed necessary, I have supplied it. I have attempted no interpretation. I am not qualified to interpret. I am qualified only to present.

My name is not important to the reader, but it will be familiar to students of competitive kendo in the postwar period. For twelve years I held the East Japan individual title. My record across sanctioned tournaments from 1971 to 1984 stood at one hundred forty-three wins, eleven losses, and one result that has no category.

The 1983 All Japan Kendo Championship final was held at the Nippon Budokan on November 3rd, a national holiday. The arena seated fourteen thousand. It was full. The tournament bracket that year placed me against six opponents in the elimination rounds. I defeated all of them. Four by ippon, two by decision. My semi-final match, against Instructor Yoshizawa of the Osaka Police Department, lasted eleven seconds.

In the opposite half of the bracket was Hideo Katsura. His elimination record that year was, as it had been in every tournament he entered, flawless. He had not lost a competitive match since 1976. His reputation does not require my description. Those who witnessed his kendo have their own memories. Those who did not will find no substitute in language.

The final was called at 3:47 in the afternoon. I took my position. I assumed my stance, chūdan-no-kamae, as I had ten thousand times. Across from me, Hideo did the same. The referee raised his flag. The command was given.

I will describe the silence that followed, because silence is the only thing I have authority over. It lasted four seconds. I know because there is a recording, and I have watched it more times than serves either my dignity or my understanding. For four seconds we stood at distance, shinai tips nearly touching. I could hear fourteen thousand people breathing.

Hideo lowered his shinai. He stepped back. He bowed—not to me, but to the shōmen, the front of the hall—and then to me, though whether the second bow was to me as opponent or me as something else I have spent forty years failing to determine. He set the shinai on the floor. He removed his men, his kote, his dō, and placed each piece beside the weapon with a precision that I recognized from his fighting. He was not performing for the crowd. He was performing his final act of technical form. Then he turned and walked through the aisle between the spectators and out of the Budokan, and the sound his bare feet made on the wooden floor was the last sound before the crowd began to react, though react is not the right word. The crowd did not react. The crowd simply came apart.

I won the All Japan Championship by forfeit. The certificate is in a box in my closet. I have never hung it.

Within a week, reports reached the kendo community that Hideo had entered Eiheiji, the great Sōtō Zen training monastery in Fukui Prefecture. Within a month, he had taken preliminary vows. Within a year, he had been ordained. He was forty-one years old and, by the consensus of every serious practitioner alive, the greatest kenshi of his generation.

Eleven months after the forfeit, the first letter arrived at my home in Sendai.

I am publishing this correspondence now, forty years later, as my final act. My doctors have used the word they use. There is time to arrange a manuscript but not to argue about one, which is why I have chosen to serve as my own editor rather than submit the letters to the university scholars who have, over the years, occasionally inquired about their existence. I told each of them that I possessed no such letters. I lied. I am not sorry. The letters were written to me, not to scholarship.

I have never understood why Hideo forfeited.

The reader may believe that statement for as long as the reader sees fit.

---

## I.

### Letter 1
#### Received December 1984. Postmarked Eiheiji, Fukui Prefecture.

The floor of the zendō is cedar, older than either of us. It is my duty this month to sweep it. The broom is made of bamboo strips bound with cord, and its sound on the wood is the only conversation I hold with regularity.

I wake at 3:40 in the morning. You may find this difficult or admirable; it is neither. It is 3:40. The bell rings and I rise. Whatever I was before 3:40 is a matter for the man lying down. The man standing up has a floor to sweep.

I write to you because there is no rule against it and because the silence here, which I chose, is different in character from the silence between us, which neither of us chose. Or rather: which I chose for both of us, which is not the same thing.

The food is adequate. The cold is not. Fukui in November has a quality of cold that is not merely temperature but opinion. The air has concluded something about your body and is uninterested in your rebuttal.

I will not apologize in this letter, or perhaps in any letter. An apology requires that one understands what one has done, and I am still sweeping.

H.

---

*[Ed. note: The letter is written on temple stationery, a thin washi paper bearing the Eiheiji crest. The handwriting, here and in the next several letters, is unmistakably Hideo's—the same hand that filled three notebooks of technical commentary now held in the Kendo Federation archives. Readers familiar with those notebooks will note that the brushwork is steadier here, less hurried. He was not writing between matches.]*

---

### Letter 2
#### Received March 1985.

It is plum blossom season. I did not know this was something that one could know—not the fact but the feel of it, the way the monastery organizes itself around the blooming as if the flowers were visiting dignitaries whose schedule must be honored. There is a plum tree in the courtyard that the abbot says is two hundred years old. I believe him. It has the posture of something that has stopped being impressed.

I have been assigned to kitchen duty. The rice is washed seven times. This is not ritual; it is practical. Improperly washed rice retains a bitterness at its center. Seven washings and the water runs clear. I mention this because I have been thinking about repetition—about acts performed so many times that the actor disappears and only the act remains. I think you would understand this. Your suburi practice was legendary even among those who hated you, and several did.

A young monk asked me today if I had done kendo. I told him I had held a sword. This was not modesty. It was the most precise language I could find.

H.

---

*[Ed. note: I did not reply to this letter or to any of the first seven. I did not know what was being asked of me. I am not certain anything was being asked.]*

---

### Letter 3
#### Received July 1985.

Summer in Fukui is the inverse of winter: the same conviction of climate, reversed in direction. The air has decided you will not be dry. Sesshin—the week of intensive meditation—is practiced in this heat, and I can report that the mind, when forced to sit absolutely still in a body that is producing water from every surface, develops opinions about the mind.

I have been reading. The library here is extensive and eccentric—a thirteenth-century manuscript beside a 1974 paperback on beekeeping, both shelved under "impermanence." I found a treatise by Yagyū Munenori, the *Heiho Kadensho*, in a copy so old the binding has been repaired with what appears to be fishing line. His discussion of *setsunintō* and *katsujinken*—the death-giving sword and the life-giving sword—is more subtle than I remembered from my student readings, when I consumed such texts as fuel rather than food.

Munenori argues that the highest use of the sword is to give life—that the warrior who has perfected killing has earned the obligation to choose when not to kill. I wonder if he believed this or if he wrote it to make the Tokugawa shōgun feel philosophical about the people he was killing.

The plum tree has finished blooming. It looks relieved.

H.

---

### Letter 4
#### Received November 1985.

The anniversary passed. I swept.

H.

---

*[Ed. note: This is the shortest letter in the collection. It is also the only letter postmarked on November 3rd itself.]*

---

### Letter 5
#### Received February 1986.

I watched two monks argue about how to stack firewood. The disagreement concerned whether the logs should be placed bark-up, to shed rain, or bark-down, to discourage insects. The argument lasted forty-five minutes. Both monks maintained absolute composure. Neither raised his voice. At the end, the senior monk said, "Let us sit with this," and they walked away from the woodpile without stacking a single log. It rained that night. The insects were not consulted.

I mention this because it has begun to remind me of certain elements of competitive kendo—the almost ceremonial refusal to resolve. You will remember the 1979 final between Instructor Morimoto and that young fighter from Tsukuba, the one whose name I cannot—Hayashida. Hayashida, yes. They circled each other for the entire regulation period without a single valid strike. Encho, the extension period, was called, and they circled for another three minutes. Morimoto won by hantei, the judges' decision, but when the flags went up, both fighters looked at the referee as if he had interrupted a conversation.

I think about Morimoto's chūdan-no-kamae sometimes. He held the shinai slightly forward of conventional center, perhaps two centimeters, enough to create a constant mild pressure on the opponent's sense of distance. It was not a flaw. It was a sentence. It said: *I am already closer than you think.*

There were other fighters whose stances spoke. Yoshizawa's jōdan was a shout. Instructor Kimura, whom I fought only once, had a kamae that said nothing at all, which was the most unnerving thing a stance could say.

Your own stance was different.

But I have spent too much of the evening on this. The abbot has asked me to assist with the calligraphy for the New Year's ceremony. My brushwork is not what it was. The cold makes the wrist unreliable.

H.

---

*[Ed. note: Hideo's analysis of Morimoto's forward-biased chūdan is, to my knowledge, original and correct. I fought Morimoto twice and can confirm the sensation he describes—a persistent feeling that distance had been subtly falsified. Hideo's observation about Kimura's silence is also precise. I note these not to validate Hideo's authority, which requires no validation, but to assure the reader that the technical content of these letters is not decorative. He saw what he saw.]*

---

### Letter 6
#### Received June 1986.

Spring cleaning at the monastery is not a metaphor. It is a man on his knees with a rag, washing five hundred years of accumulated reverence off the floor. The reverence, it turns out, leaves a residue not unlike cooking grease.

I have been thinking about what I did not finish saying in my last letter—about stances that speak. This is not mysticism. A stance is a physical argument about where the body expects danger and where it expects opportunity. Every kamae is a prediction: here is where I believe you will strike, and here is where I believe I can answer. To read a stance is to read a mind, or at least that portion of the mind that the body has been trained to externalize.

When I was competing I developed a habit—a weakness, perhaps—of reading too quickly. I would see the stance and know the fighter within the first two seconds. This was useful. It was also, I have come to believe, a form of discourtesy, though I could not have articulated this at the time. To see someone completely before they have chosen to be seen—there is something violent in it, even without a sword.

H.

---

### Letter 7
#### Received October 1986.

Your stance.

I should say this plainly, or as plainly as I am presently able: your chūdan-no-kamae was the most beautiful I encountered in twenty years of competition. I do not use this word lightly or aesthetically. I mean that it was *correct* in the way that certain mathematical proofs are correct—not merely functional but necessary, each element in its only possible position. The grip, the distance between your hands, the particular angle at which you held the shinai's tip relative to your opponent's throat: these were not style. They were architecture.

I have seen fighters with faster reflexes. I have seen fighters with greater physical power. I have never seen a fighter whose kamae was so fully resolved. When you settled into your stance, the match became a problem that you had already structured in your favor. Your opponents felt this. I watched them feel it—the slight hesitation, the barely perceptible recalibration of ambition that occurred in the first half-second of facing you. They did not know what they were responding to. They felt the building and did not have the language for

I have been repairing a section of the garden wall today, fitting stones without mortar, and I find that this work occupies the same part of the mind as what I am trying to say to you, so I will describe it instead. Each stone must be placed so that its weight is carried by the stones beneath it and the stones beside it. There is no adhesive. There is only the rightness of position. When a stone is correctly placed, you can feel it settle—not with a sound but with an absence of sound, a cessation of the small grinding that indicates misalignment. Your stance was like that. Your whole kamae settled into itself with a silence that I have never

The second page of this letter concerns the garden wall, which I have been repairing all week. The maple beside it has begun to turn. Autumn in Fukui arrives as a kind of apology for summer.

H.

---

*[Ed. note: Here the reader will note that the letter continues on a second page, which discusses the temple garden. I have chosen to include both pages.]*

---

### Letter 8
#### Received March 1987.

The plum tree is blooming again. I begin to understand the monks' reverence for it. It is not that the blossoms are beautiful, though they are. It is that the tree undertakes the same action each year without appearing to deliberate. It is not brave. Bravery requires the possibility of refusal. The tree has no such possibility. It blooms because it is a plum tree. I envy it.

I have received a letter from the Kendo Federation asking whether I would contribute a technical essay to their anniversary publication. I declined. I am not certain I declined for the right reasons.

This morning during zazen I found myself counting breaths and realized I was counting in the rhythm of kakari-geiko—the rapid striking drill, one-two-one-two, attack without thinking. The body does not forget. It merely waits.

The abbot told me something last week that I have been turning over: "The obstacle is not between you and the truth. The obstacle is your preference for the obstacle." I asked him what this meant. He said, "You already know, which is why you asked."

I do not find Zen masters as helpful as their reputation suggests.

H.

---

*[Ed. note: The Kendo Federation confirms that they invited Hideo to contribute to their 40th anniversary publication in 1987. They also invited me. I contributed a short technical piece on attacking from the center. I did not know they had also contacted Hideo. I have wondered, since discovering this, whether my essay was read at Eiheiji. I have no evidence either way.]*

## II.

---

### Letter 9
#### Received January 1988.

I have been reading the Hagakure again. Tsunetomo's famous declaration—"The Way of the Warrior is found in death"—is typically read as an injunction to fearlessness: be prepared to die, and you will fight without hesitation. But I read it now as something else. Tsunetomo was not a warrior. He was a retainer who was forbidden by law to follow his lord in death, and who spent the rest of his life dictating his philosophy to a scribe. The Hagakure is the work of a man who was denied the defining action of his value system. Everything in it is therefore written by an exile, about exile, and the philosophy it produces is the philosophy of a man who must make meaning from the refusal of the act that would have given his life its meaning.
